case_info.scenario: A 67-year-old man with thoracolumbar scoliosis, poor mobility, and history of frequent falls presented to the emergency department with 2 months of left shoulder pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion, and numbness and paresthesias in his left upper extremity. Ten years prior to presentation, he underwent surgical decompression for syringomyelia. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of his cervical and thoracic spine performed 2 years prior to presentation revealed a recurrent syrinx extending from C1 to T11, which was not resected because it did not cause symptoms at that time. On physical examination, he had mild tenderness to palpation and reduced range of motion of the left shoulder with abduction and flexion limited to 120° (normal range of motion, 180°). The left scapular muscles were atrophic, and pain and temperature sensation were reduced in his proximal left arm, and dorsal aspect of his left shoulder. His complete blood cell count, serum glucose levels, C-reactive protein levels, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody were negative. Left shoulder radiograph showed complete absence of the left humeral head and a well-demarcated smooth osseous margin of the proximal humerus with associated soft tissue swelling and periarticular calcification (Figure 1). A chest radiograph taken 2 years prior revealed a normal left shoulder joint. The patient was hospitalized for further evaluation and treatment.

case_info.explanation: Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder (Charcot shoulder) A. Obtain MRI of the left shoulder The key to the correct diagnosis of neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder is the radiographic finding of an absent left humeral head in a patient with a history of syringomyelia. Choices B and D are incorrect because the well-defined linear margins of the proximal humerus made septic arthritis or osteolysis due to malignancy unlikely. Shoulder replacement surgery (choice C) is not recommended for most patients with Charcot shoulder. Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder joint, also known as Charcot shoulder, is a rare progressive disorder characterized by rapid joint destruction and associated soft tissue swelling.1,2Patients typically present with gradually increasing shoulder swelling, which may or may not be painful, weakness in the shoulder, and decreased range of motion of the shoulder. Patients may report paresthesias or numbness in the affected upper extremity.1,2Approximately 80% of people with Charcot shoulder have syringomyelia, characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the spinal cord.2Other conditions associated with Charcot shoulder include diabetes, syphilis, alcohol use disorder, Arnold-Chiari malformations, cervical spondylosis, amyloidosis, end-stage kidney disease, myelodysplasia, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, intra-articular steroid injection, tuberculosis, leprosy (Hansen disease), and gigantism.2-4 Syringomyelia may be congenital or secondary to trauma, infection, tumors, vascular abnormalities, or spinal degeneration.4As it expands, a syrinx damages spinothalamic tract fibers and may compress dorsal column and anterior horn cells, resulting in loss of sensation of pain and temperature, decreased muscle strength, muscle atrophy, and arreflexia.5,6Approximately 6% of patients with syringomyelia develop Charcot shoulder, and 80% have involvement of only 1 joint.1,6 The pathophysiology of neuropathic arthropathy, such as Charcot shoulder, is incompletely understood. A syrinx may decrease shoulder joint sensory innervation, leading to loss of somatic muscle reflexes that protect the joint from injury, resulting in recurrent subclinical trauma that causes inflammation and progressive shoulder joint destruction.2,6A syrinx may also cause loss of autonomic vascular control, increasing blood flow to the joint, and activating osteoclasts, which results in accelerated bone resorption.1,7 Patients with Charcot shoulder may have atrophic changes on radiographs, consisting of substantial bone resorption or shoulder joint destruction, and hypertrophic reactions, with osteophytes, sclerosis, and accumulation of osseous debris.2MRI of the shoulder can confirm the presence of Charcot shoulder and facilitates assessments for other associated conditions, such as rotator cuff tear.2 The diagnosis of Charcot shoulder should be made only after exclusion of other causes of joint destruction, including septic arthritis, osteolytic lesions from malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, synovial chondromatosis, trauma, soft tissue sarcoma, and Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a destructive arthropathy caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals.1,3 Upon diagnosis of Charcot shoulder, the underlying cause should be identified and treated, in an attempt to slow or halt further joint destruction. Surgical resection of a syrinx in patients with Charcot shoulder due to syringomyelia may slow joint deterioration and improve neurologic symptoms.2Treatments for Charcot shoulder include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, joint aspiration if an effusion is present, patient education about avoidance of mechanical trauma, physical therapy, and rehabiliation.1-3Shoulder surgery is not typically recommended, but may be considered for a subset of patients with Charcot shoulder who do not improve with nonoperative management.2,7 The patient was treated with acetaminophen (paracetamol), topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and short-acting opioids as needed. MRI showed destructive osteolysis of the left humeral head with well-defined, linearly demarcated margins of the proximal humerus with surrounding osseous debris and a moderate glenohumeral joint effusion (Figure 2). After consultation by clinicians in neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery, geriatrics, and radiology, the patient was advised to undergo intensive physical and occupational therapy. After 4 weeks of inpatient physical therapy 5 days per week, his left shoulder pain resolved, and left shoulder flexion and abduction was 160° to 170°. At his most recent outpatient clinic visit, 3 months after hospital discharge, the patient reported no left shoulder pain and had no change in shoulder range of motion. A follow up radiograph revealed a slight decrease in the left glenohumeral effusion.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder (Charcot shoulder) A. Obtain MRI of the left shoulder The key to the correct diagnosis of neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder is the radiographic finding of an absent left humeral head in a patient with a history of syringomyelia. Choices B and D are incorrect because the well-defined linear margins of the proximal humerus made septic arthritis or osteolysis due to malignancy unlikely. Shoulder replacement surgery (choice C) is not recommended for most patients with Charcot shoulder. Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder joint, also known as Charcot shoulder, is a rare progressive disorder characterized by rapid joint destruction and associated soft tissue swelling.1,2Patients typically present with gradually increasing shoulder swelling, which may or may not be painful, weakness in the shoulder, and decreased range of motion of the shoulder. Patients may report paresthesias or numbness in the affected upper extremity.1,2Approximately 80% of people with Charcot shoulder have syringomyelia, characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the spinal cord.2Other conditions associated with Charcot shoulder include diabetes, syphilis, alcohol use disorder, Arnold-Chiari malformations, cervical spondylosis, amyloidosis, end-stage kidney disease, myelodysplasia, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, intra-articular steroid injection, tuberculosis, leprosy (Hansen disease), and gigantism.2-4 Syringomyelia may be congenital or secondary to trauma, infection, tumors, vascular abnormalities, or spinal degeneration.4As it expands, a syrinx damages spinothalamic tract fibers and may compress dorsal column and anterior horn cells, resulting in loss of sensation of pain and temperature, decreased muscle strength, muscle atrophy, and arreflexia.5,6Approximately 6% of patients with syringomyelia develop Charcot shoulder, and 80% have involvement of only 1 joint.1,6 The pathophysiology of neuropathic arthropathy, such as Charcot shoulder, is incompletely understood. A syrinx may decrease shoulder joint sensory innervation, leading to loss of somatic muscle reflexes that protect the joint from injury, resulting in recurrent subclinical trauma that causes inflammation and progressive shoulder joint destruction.2,6A syrinx may also cause loss of autonomic vascular control, increasing blood flow to the joint, and activating osteoclasts, which results in accelerated bone resorption.1,7 Patients with Charcot shoulder may have atrophic changes on radiographs, consisting of substantial bone resorption or shoulder joint destruction, and hypertrophic reactions, with osteophytes, sclerosis, and accumulation of osseous debris.2MRI of the shoulder can confirm the presence of Charcot shoulder and facilitates assessments for other associated conditions, such as rotator cuff tear.2 The diagnosis of Charcot shoulder should be made only after exclusion of other causes of joint destruction, including septic arthritis, osteolytic lesions from malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, synovial chondromatosis, trauma, soft tissue sarcoma, and Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a destructive arthropathy caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals.1,3 Upon diagnosis of Charcot shoulder, the underlying cause should be identified and treated, in an attempt to slow or halt further joint destruction. Surgical resection of a syrinx in patients with Charcot shoulder due to syringomyelia may slow joint deterioration and improve neurologic symptoms.2Treatments for Charcot shoulder include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, joint aspiration if an effusion is present, patient education about avoidance of mechanical trauma, physical therapy, and rehabiliation.1-3Shoulder surgery is not typically recommended, but may be considered for a subset of patients with Charcot shoulder who do not improve with nonoperative management.2,7 The patient was treated with acetaminophen (paracetamol), topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and short-acting opioids as needed. MRI showed destructive osteolysis of the left humeral head with well-defined, linearly demarcated margins of the proximal humerus with surrounding osseous debris and a moderate glenohumeral joint effusion (Figure 2). After consultation by clinicians in neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery, geriatrics, and radiology, the patient was advised to undergo intensive physical and occupational therapy. After 4 weeks of inpatient physical therapy 5 days per week, his left shoulder pain resolved, and left shoulder flexion and abduction was 160° to 170°. At his most recent outpatient clinic visit, 3 months after hospital discharge, the patient reported no left shoulder pain and had no change in shoulder range of motion. A follow up radiograph revealed a slight decrease in the left glenohumeral effusion.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder (Charcot shoulder) A. Obtain MRI of the left shoulder The key to the correct diagnosis of neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder is the radiographic finding of an absent left humeral head in a patient with a history of syringomyelia. Choices B and D are incorrect because the well-defined linear margins of the proximal humerus made septic arthritis or osteolysis due to malignancy unlikely. Shoulder replacement surgery (choice C) is not recommended for most patients with Charcot shoulder. Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder joint, also known as Charcot shoulder, is a rare progressive disorder characterized by rapid joint destruction and associated soft tissue swelling.1,2Patients typically present with gradually increasing shoulder swelling, which may or may not be painful, weakness in the shoulder, and decreased range of motion of the shoulder. Patients may report paresthesias or numbness in the affected upper extremity.1,2Approximately 80% of people with Charcot shoulder have syringomyelia, characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the spinal cord.2Other conditions associated with Charcot shoulder include diabetes, syphilis, alcohol use disorder, Arnold-Chiari malformations, cervical spondylosis, amyloidosis, end-stage kidney disease, myelodysplasia, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, intra-articular steroid injection, tuberculosis, leprosy (Hansen disease), and gigantism.2-4 Syringomyelia may be congenital or secondary to trauma, infection, tumors, vascular abnormalities, or spinal degeneration.4As it expands, a syrinx damages spinothalamic tract fibers and may compress dorsal column and anterior horn cells, resulting in loss of sensation of pain and temperature, decreased muscle strength, muscle atrophy, and arreflexia.5,6Approximately 6% of patients with syringomyelia develop Charcot shoulder, and 80% have involvement of only 1 joint.1,6 The pathophysiology of neuropathic arthropathy, such as Charcot shoulder, is incompletely understood. A syrinx may decrease shoulder joint sensory innervation, leading to loss of somatic muscle reflexes that protect the joint from injury, resulting in recurrent subclinical trauma that causes inflammation and progressive shoulder joint destruction.2,6A syrinx may also cause loss of autonomic vascular control, increasing blood flow to the joint, and activating osteoclasts, which results in accelerated bone resorption.1,7 Patients with Charcot shoulder may have atrophic changes on radiographs, consisting of substantial bone resorption or shoulder joint destruction, and hypertrophic reactions, with osteophytes, sclerosis, and accumulation of osseous debris.2MRI of the shoulder can confirm the presence of Charcot shoulder and facilitates assessments for other associated conditions, such as rotator cuff tear.2 The diagnosis of Charcot shoulder should be made only after exclusion of other causes of joint destruction, including septic arthritis, osteolytic lesions from malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, synovial chondromatosis, trauma, soft tissue sarcoma, and Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a destructive arthropathy caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals.1,3 Upon diagnosis of Charcot shoulder, the underlying cause should be identified and treated, in an attempt to slow or halt further joint destruction. Surgical resection of a syrinx in patients with Charcot shoulder due to syringomyelia may slow joint deterioration and improve neurologic symptoms.2Treatments for Charcot shoulder include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, joint aspiration if an effusion is present, patient education about avoidance of mechanical trauma, physical therapy, and rehabiliation.1-3Shoulder surgery is not typically recommended, but may be considered for a subset of patients with Charcot shoulder who do not improve with nonoperative management.2,7 The patient was treated with acetaminophen (paracetamol), topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and short-acting opioids as needed. MRI showed destructive osteolysis of the left humeral head with well-defined, linearly demarcated margins of the proximal humerus with surrounding osseous debris and a moderate glenohumeral joint effusion (Figure 2). After consultation by clinicians in neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery, geriatrics, and radiology, the patient was advised to undergo intensive physical and occupational therapy. After 4 weeks of inpatient physical therapy 5 days per week, his left shoulder pain resolved, and left shoulder flexion and abduction was 160° to 170°. At his most recent outpatient clinic visit, 3 months after hospital discharge, the patient reported no left shoulder pain and had no change in shoulder range of motion. A follow up radiograph revealed a slight decrease in the left glenohumeral effusion.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

2. Performance

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort

case_info.explanation: Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder (Charcot shoulder) A. Obtain MRI of the left shoulder The key to the correct diagnosis of neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder is the radiographic finding of an absent left humeral head in a patient with a history of syringomyelia. Choices B and D are incorrect because the well-defined linear margins of the proximal humerus made septic arthritis or osteolysis due to malignancy unlikely. Shoulder replacement surgery (choice C) is not recommended for most patients with Charcot shoulder. Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder joint, also known as Charcot shoulder, is a rare progressive disorder characterized by rapid joint destruction and associated soft tissue swelling.1,2Patients typically present with gradually increasing shoulder swelling, which may or may not be painful, weakness in the shoulder, and decreased range of motion of the shoulder. Patients may report paresthesias or numbness in the affected upper extremity.1,2Approximately 80% of people with Charcot shoulder have syringomyelia, characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the spinal cord.2Other conditions associated with Charcot shoulder include diabetes, syphilis, alcohol use disorder, Arnold-Chiari malformations, cervical spondylosis, amyloidosis, end-stage kidney disease, myelodysplasia, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, intra-articular steroid injection, tuberculosis, leprosy (Hansen disease), and gigantism.2-4 Syringomyelia may be congenital or secondary to trauma, infection, tumors, vascular abnormalities, or spinal degeneration.4As it expands, a syrinx damages spinothalamic tract fibers and may compress dorsal column and anterior horn cells, resulting in loss of sensation of pain and temperature, decreased muscle strength, muscle atrophy, and arreflexia.5,6Approximately 6% of patients with syringomyelia develop Charcot shoulder, and 80% have involvement of only 1 joint.1,6 The pathophysiology of neuropathic arthropathy, such as Charcot shoulder, is incompletely understood. A syrinx may decrease shoulder joint sensory innervation, leading to loss of somatic muscle reflexes that protect the joint from injury, resulting in recurrent subclinical trauma that causes inflammation and progressive shoulder joint destruction.2,6A syrinx may also cause loss of autonomic vascular control, increasing blood flow to the joint, and activating osteoclasts, which results in accelerated bone resorption.1,7 Patients with Charcot shoulder may have atrophic changes on radiographs, consisting of substantial bone resorption or shoulder joint destruction, and hypertrophic reactions, with osteophytes, sclerosis, and accumulation of osseous debris.2MRI of the shoulder can confirm the presence of Charcot shoulder and facilitates assessments for other associated conditions, such as rotator cuff tear.2 The diagnosis of Charcot shoulder should be made only after exclusion of other causes of joint destruction, including septic arthritis, osteolytic lesions from malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, synovial chondromatosis, trauma, soft tissue sarcoma, and Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a destructive arthropathy caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals.1,3 Upon diagnosis of Charcot shoulder, the underlying cause should be identified and treated, in an attempt to slow or halt further joint destruction. Surgical resection of a syrinx in patients with Charcot shoulder due to syringomyelia may slow joint deterioration and improve neurologic symptoms.2Treatments for Charcot shoulder include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, joint aspiration if an effusion is present, patient education about avoidance of mechanical trauma, physical therapy, and rehabiliation.1-3Shoulder surgery is not typically recommended, but may be considered for a subset of patients with Charcot shoulder who do not improve with nonoperative management.2,7 The patient was treated with acetaminophen (paracetamol), topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and short-acting opioids as needed. MRI showed destructive osteolysis of the left humeral head with well-defined, linearly demarcated margins of the proximal humerus with surrounding osseous debris and a moderate glenohumeral joint effusion (Figure 2). You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{

  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 67-year-old man with thoracolumbar scoliosis, poor mobility, and history of frequent falls presented to the emergency department with 2 months of left shoulder pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion, and numbness and paresthesias in his left upper extremity. Ten years prior to presentation, he underwent surgical decompression for syringomyelia. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of his cervical and thoracic spine performed 2 years prior to presentation revealed a recurrent syrinx extending from C1 to T11, which was not resected because it did not cause symptoms at that time. On physical examination, he had mild tenderness to palpation and reduced range of motion of the left shoulder with abduction and flexion limited to 120° (normal range of motion, 180°). The left scapular muscles were atrophic, and pain and temperature sensation were reduced in his proximal left arm, and dorsal aspect of his left shoulder. His complete blood cell count, serum glucose levels, C-reactive protein levels, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody were negative. Left shoulder radiograph showed complete absence of the left humeral head and a well-demarcated smooth osseous margin of the proximal humerus with associated soft tissue swelling and periarticular calcification (Figure 1). A chest radiograph taken 2 years prior revealed a normal left shoulder joint. The patient was hospitalized for further evaluation and treatment.

case_info.explanation: Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder (Charcot shoulder) A. Obtain MRI of the left shoulder The key to the correct diagnosis of neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder is the radiographic finding of an absent left humeral head in a patient with a history of syringomyelia. Choices B and D are incorrect because the well-defined linear margins of the proximal humerus made septic arthritis or osteolysis due to malignancy unlikely. Shoulder replacement surgery (choice C) is not recommended for most patients with Charcot shoulder. Neuropathic arthropathy of the shoulder joint, also known as Charcot shoulder, is a rare progressive disorder characterized by rapid joint destruction and associated soft tissue swelling.1,2Patients typically present with gradually increasing shoulder swelling, which may or may not be painful, weakness in the shoulder, and decreased range of motion of the shoulder. Patients may report paresthesias or numbness in the affected upper extremity.1,2Approximately 80% of people with Charcot shoulder have syringomyelia, characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the spinal cord.2Other conditions associated with Charcot shoulder include diabetes, syphilis, alcohol use disorder, Arnold-Chiari malformations, cervical spondylosis, amyloidosis, end-stage kidney disease, myelodysplasia, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, intra-articular steroid injection, tuberculosis, leprosy (Hansen disease), and gigantism.2-4 Syringomyelia may be congenital or secondary to trauma, infection, tumors, vascular abnormalities, or spinal degeneration.4As it expands, a syrinx damages spinothalamic tract fibers and may compress dorsal column and anterior horn cells, resulting in loss of sensation of pain and temperature, decreased muscle strength, muscle atrophy, and arreflexia.5,6Approximately 6% of patients with syringomyelia develop Charcot shoulder, and 80% have involvement of only 1 joint.1,6 The pathophysiology of neuropathic arthropathy, such as Charcot shoulder, is incompletely understood. A syrinx may decrease shoulder joint sensory innervation, leading to loss of somatic muscle reflexes that protect the joint from injury, resulting in recurrent subclinical trauma that causes inflammation and progressive shoulder joint destruction.2,6A syrinx may also cause loss of autonomic vascular control, increasing blood flow to the joint, and activating osteoclasts, which results in accelerated bone resorption.1,7 Patients with Charcot shoulder may have atrophic changes on radiographs, consisting of substantial bone resorption or shoulder joint destruction, and hypertrophic reactions, with osteophytes, sclerosis, and accumulation of osseous debris.2MRI of the shoulder can confirm the presence of Charcot shoulder and facilitates assessments for other associated conditions, such as rotator cuff tear.2 The diagnosis of Charcot shoulder should be made only after exclusion of other causes of joint destruction, including septic arthritis, osteolytic lesions from malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, synovial chondromatosis, trauma, soft tissue sarcoma, and Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a destructive arthropathy caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals.1,3 Upon diagnosis of Charcot shoulder, the underlying cause should be identified and treated, in an attempt to slow or halt further joint destruction. Surgical resection of a syrinx in patients with Charcot shoulder due to syringomyelia may slow joint deterioration and improve neurologic symptoms.2Treatments for Charcot shoulder include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, joint aspiration if an effusion is present, patient education about avoidance of mechanical trauma, physical therapy, and rehabiliation.1-3Shoulder surgery is not typically recommended, but may be considered for a subset of patients with Charcot shoulder who do not improve with nonoperative management.2,7 The patient was treated with acetaminophen (paracetamol), topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and short-acting opioids as needed. MRI showed destructive osteolysis of the left humeral head with well-defined, linearly demarcated margins of the proximal humerus with surrounding osseous debris and a moderate glenohumeral joint effusion (Figure 2). After consultation by clinicians in neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery, geriatrics, and radiology, the patient was advised to undergo intensive physical and occupational therapy. After 4 weeks of inpatient physical therapy 5 days per week, his left shoulder pain resolved, and left shoulder flexion and abduction was 160° to 170°. At his most recent outpatient clinic visit, 3 months after hospital discharge, the patient reported no left shoulder pain and had no change in shoulder range of motion. A follow up radiograph revealed a slight decrease in the left glenohumeral effusion.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.
